newsitem.title: USA: Girls weak in science, Asian nations tops - study.
newsitem.headline: Girls weak in science, Asian nations tops - study.

text.p: A study of education in 45 countries released on Wednesday found that 13-year-old girls were not very good at science, and students in Asian nations were the best.
While gender differences were minimal in mathematics, they were pervasive in science, the Third International Mathematics and Science Study involving 500,000 students showed.

"Boys outperformed girls, particularly in physics, chemistry and Earth science," the study's director, Dr. Albert Beaton said. "As we move into a more technology-based, science driven world, girls' economic options will be affected."

The study, headquartered at Boston College and conducted under the auspices of the Netherlands-based International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement, evaluated three age groups of students and released the results of those dealing with 13-year-olds.
Singapore was the top-performing country in both science and math at the seventh and eighth grades, the study found. South Korea, Japan and the Czech Republic also did very well.

The United States, England and New Zealand finished in the bottom-half of the 45 nations in mathematics in both grades, though England and the United States did better in science. South Africa was the worst performing country in both mathematics and science.
"I wish I could say it was as simple as saying give all the kids calculators, because in all the countries where they used calculators, the students did well," said Beaton.
"But then you have (South) Korea, where they don't use calculators, but nonetheless managed to rank second in both grades in mathematics."

Class size could also be expected to play a big role in education, but again South Korea proved the contrary, the study showed. In a number of countries nearly all students were in classes of fewer than 30 students, but in South Korea, class size was regularly more than 40 students.
"One of the more interesting aspects is that students all over the world who have television spend about the same amount of time watching it -- about two hours a day," Beaton said.
